classification.tone: Grounded, paranoid, escalating, with surreal cosmic dread

evaluation.positioning_hook: An FBI agent tailing missing ex-cons in Silver Lake stumbles into a comet-fueled underground conspiracy, where the real predators are the people watching from the next house over.

audience_appeal_marketability.reasoning: The hook is immediate and easy to sell: an FBI surveillance sting, a neighborhood mystery, and a cosmic event all collide in a way that feels built for genre audiences. The opening van stakeout, the red-door/blue-door split, and the final reveal of a hidden feeding system give it strong trailer moments and a clear commercial promise.

conceptual_hook_clarity.reasoning: The premise lands early and cleanly: Rico tracks missing ex-cons, bugs the wrong house, and discovers a second house with a concealed dungeon and a larger system behind it. The red-door/blue-door geography, the comet countdown, and the surveillance setup make the engine legible without over-explaining.

character_appeal_and_long_term_potential.reasoning: Rico has a strong internal engine because her professional certainty and childhood wound keep colliding, especially once the mother disappearance story folds into the case. Cole gives the script a sturdy partner dynamic, and Watson’s calm authority turns into a memorable antagonist, though the supporting players mostly serve the central mystery.

creative_originality_and_boldness.reasoning: The script takes a familiar surveillance-thriller frame and pushes it into a comet-driven, tinfoil-lined subterranean nightmare with a very specific visual language. The red-door/blue-door split, the ASMR eating motif, and the bureaucratic horror of the FBI cover-up give it a confident, off-center identity.

narrative_momentum_engagement.reasoning: The story keeps escalating through discoveries, reversals, and betrayals, with each act revealing a deeper layer of the same neighborhood. The switch from stakeout to hidden bunker to institutional conspiracy gives the feature a strong forward pull and a climax that pays off the setup.

resonant_originality.reasoning: The script feels like it has found a fresh mythic engine: missing ex-cons, a comet, and a hidden feeding system that turns surveillance itself into complicity. The idea that the FBI’s best month is built on a secret predation system is both immediate and memorable.

world_density_and_texture.reasoning: The LA neighborhood, the FBI field office, the support group, and the hidden house system all feel specific and story-generating. The world is strongest when it leans into procedural bureaucracy and suburban concealment, though the larger mythology stays mostly in service of the plot.

tonal_specificity.reasoning: The tone is unusually specific: procedural banter, deadpan workplace friction, cosmic paranoia, and body-horror escalation all coexist without losing the script’s voice. The eating sounds, the bell, the foil, and the comet imagery create a tonal signature that would be recognizable in a single scene.

latent_depth_slow_burn_potential.reasoning: Beneath the thriller mechanics, the script keeps opening into grief, memory, institutional denial, and the way people build stories to survive loss. Rico’s mother wound and Watson’s system-level worldview give the material more depth than a standard conspiracy thriller, even as the feature stays tightly plot-driven.

relationship_density_and_ensemble_engine.reasoning: Rico and Cole have the strongest recurring dynamic, and Watson adds a second strong axis, but the script is still primarily powered by Rico’s perspective. The supporting relationships are effective and memorable, though the feature lives more on the lead’s journey than on a broad ensemble web.

casting_characteristics: Two adult male supporting roles with strong contrast
One child version of the protagonist in flashback

locations.interior_exterior_ratio: Mostly interior with some exterior night work
notable_requirements: Residential neighborhood with two adjacent houses and shared garage

technical.vfx_details: Comet imagery, sky glow, final meteorite devastation, and a few subjective light effects; most of the horror is practical and editorially driven.
technical.sfx_needs: Blood, body-horror makeup, foil-wrapped creature effects, seizure effects, gunfire, and practical destruction in the climax.

rights_flags.detail: Patriot Act, NSA, FBI, LAPD, Reynolds Wrap, Bud Light, QuickTime Player, Pelican case, Taco Stand, Honda Civic, Shih Tzu, Minute Maid, and other named consumer or institutional references appear on the page.
No real people are referenced by name.
No external IP is required beyond incidental brand and institutional references.

platform_fit.recommended_lane: Streaming feature or premium genre label
platform_fit.series_engine_or_release_model: Best suited to a festival-to-platform or direct-streaming release model as a contained genre feature.

cost.note: The core footprint is contained to offices, a van, and two neighboring houses, but the climax adds creature effects, blood, and comet-driven destruction.

cast.note: The project depends on a strong lead for Rico, a memorable older partner in Cole, and a commanding authority figure in Watson, with a handful of supporting roles that matter to the twist.

location.note: Most of the story lives in a compact neighborhood and a few interiors, though the night exteriors, basement build, and Bora Bora coda add some scope.

content.note: The script includes blood, mutilation, body horror, implied torture, gun violence, and a final creature reveal that pushes it firmly into mature territory.

rights.note: The script uses mostly generic or incidental references, with no major life-rights or music-clearance dependency.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The red-door/blue-door setup is instantly ownable.
strengths.what_it_means: That visual rule gives the movie a clean marketing image and a simple audience-facing mystery that can be sold in one sentence. Thriller buyers and genre actors will respond to a premise that is both easy to grasp and loaded with dread.
strengths.evidence: The two identical houses differentiated only by their red and blue front doors, with the story built around which house contains the hidden operation.

strengths.dimension_or_area: Rico is built around grief and professional hunger.
strengths.what_it_means: The role gives an actress a procedural lead with emotional fracture underneath, which is the kind of part that can anchor a genre feature and still feel awards-adjacent. Mid-career dramatic leads and actors looking for a smart, physical, emotionally loaded thriller role will chase this.
strengths.evidence: Rico’s obsession with the missing-person memory of her mother keeps colliding with her FBI work, especially in the flashbacks and the support-group material with James.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The workplace banter has real personality.
strengths.what_it_means: Cole’s eating, Rico’s irritation, and Watson’s bell create a lived-in bureau rhythm that makes the movie feel like a place, not just a plot machine. Character actors and directors who like procedural texture will see a lot to play in the office and van scenes.
strengths.evidence: The opening FBI office sequence, the cup-o-noodles bit, the taco run, and the bell that controls the room.

strengths.what_it_means: The script turns paperwork, warrants, surveillance, and chain-of-command into part of the terror, which gives the genre a fresh institutional angle. Buyers who like elevated genre and actors who enjoy playing authority, denial, and complicity will notice that immediately.
strengths.evidence: Watson repeatedly delays action, invokes title three and warrants, and later reveals the system is being used to manage the creatures.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The sound design is baked into the concept.
strengths.what_it_means: The eating noises, the bell, the high-pitched ringing, and the comet hum all suggest a movie that can be terrifying with sound alone, which is a real trailer and theatrical asset. Horror-forward directors and sound-driven genre buyers will see a strong signature here.
strengths.evidence: Cole’s chewing, Henry’s slurping, the bell, the whine that accompanies the creatures, and Rico’s recurring ear-piercing episodes.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The final reveal reframes the whole case.
strengths.what_it_means: The underground feeding system and Watson’s role in it turn the feature from a missing-person thriller into a conspiracy horror with a clean, shocking payoff. Genre buyers and audience-facing stars will like that the movie keeps opening up rather than simply resolving the initial case.
strengths.evidence: The dungeon, the foil-lined rooms, the creature forms, and Watson’s explanation that the system feeds on ex-cons and is managed through the bureau.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The comet gives the story a mythic clock.
strengths.what_it_means: The astronomical countdown adds scale without requiring a giant production footprint, and it gives the movie a built-in deadline that feels bigger than the neighborhood. Streamers and theatrical genre buyers alike can use that countdown as a clean suspense engine.
strengths.evidence: Comet Theora’s approach, the forum research, the five-day countdown, and the final convergence as the comet reaches Earth.

whats_special.headline: This is a contained genre feature with a sharp visual hook, a strong lead role, and a conspiracy engine that keeps widening until it becomes something stranger and more dangerous. The movie’s best asset is how it turns ordinary surveillance into cosmic dread: a neighborhood stakeout becomes a hidden feeding system, and an FBI agent’s personal grief becomes the key to the whole nightmare.

lead_characters.name: Lucía Del Rico
lead_characters.hook: Rico is a sharp, restless FBI agent whose competence is always fighting with her private obsession. She reads as hyper-alert and professionally hungry, but the script keeps revealing a woman whose need to make sense of the world is rooted in a childhood disappearance she never got over.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the showcase territory of Jodie Foster in The Silence of the Lambs — a disciplined investigator whose intelligence is inseparable from vulnerability and pressure. It gives an actor the chance to play procedural authority, emotional fracture, and escalating physical danger in one role, which is exactly the kind of part prestige leads and genre-savvy stars pursue.

lead_characters.name: Dale Cole
lead_characters.hook: Cole is the veteran agent who looks like he’s already halfway out the door, but keeps proving he still knows how the room works. He’s dry, world-weary, and unexpectedly generous, with a lived-in cynicism that turns into real emotional ballast for Rico.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the showcase territory of Tommy Lee Jones in No Country for Old Men — an older professional whose authority comes from understatement, timing, and accumulated fatigue. It gives a seasoned actor a role that can play comic irritation, mentor energy, and late-career moral clarity without ever leaving the genre lane.

lead_characters.name: Captain Watson
lead_characters.hook: Watson is all institutional polish on the surface, the kind of boss who can turn a bell and a smile into a room full of obedience. He carries himself like a protector of the public, but the script steadily reveals a man who has turned procedure into a predatory system.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the showcase territory of Bryan Cranston in Breaking Bad when authority and menace are fused into one calm performance. It gives an actor the chance to play charm, command, and concealed monstrosity in a role that can dominate the movie without ever raising its voice.

lead_characters.name: James White
lead_characters.hook: James is the grief-group outsider who seems tender, awkward, and emotionally available until the script reveals how deeply he’s already been pulled into the system. He functions as both a romantic pressure point and a tragic mirror for Rico, which makes him feel like more than a simple supporting player.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the showcase territory of Jake Gyllenhaal in Nightcrawler — a character whose softness and intensity keep shifting under the audience’s feet. It gives an actor the chance to play intimacy, concealment, and eventual horror in a role that starts human and ends as something far stranger.

lead_characters.name: Henry Dodson
lead_characters.hook: Henry is the first suspect who seems like a menace, then becomes something more complicated: a frightened, compromised man trying to survive a system he half understands. He’s twitchy, observant, and weirdly polite, which makes him feel dangerous even when he’s trying to warn Rico.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the showcase territory of Ben Mendelsohn in Animal Kingdom — a man whose menace comes wrapped in exhaustion, intelligence, and damage. It gives a character actor a role with real tonal range: suspect, victim, informant, and doomed witness all in one part.

lead_characters.name: Hope
lead_characters.hook: Hope is serene, eerie, and almost devotional in the way she speaks about the comet and the days ahead. She feels like someone who has accepted a private apocalypse and is trying to keep the household calm until it arrives.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the showcase territory of Toni Collette in Hereditary — a woman whose stillness and certainty become terrifying once the audience understands what she’s carrying. It gives an actress a role that can play domestic calm, spiritual dread, and body-horror transformation.

lead_characters.name: Lear
lead_characters.hook: Lear is the quieter half of the couple, the one who seems to manage the practical side of their strange domestic ritual. He’s anxious, compliant, and increasingly unsettling as the house’s hidden logic becomes clearer.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the showcase territory of Michael Shannon in Take Shelter — a man whose fear is visible even when he’s trying to act normal. It gives an actor the chance to play domestic unease, loyalty, and eventual physical transformation with a strong genre hook.

lead_characters.name: Marissa
lead_characters.hook: Marissa is the support-group facilitator who gives the movie a brief, grounded social frame outside the FBI and the conspiracy. She’s calm, empathetic, and functional, serving as the bridge between grief and the larger mystery.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of grounded supporting role that works in the Frances McDormand in Nomadland lane — a calm, observant presence that gives the film emotional credibility. Character actors who like to anchor scenes with authority and warmth would be interested.

lead_characters.name: Isaac Martinez
lead_characters.hook: Isaac is the first visible victim and the script’s clearest example of how the system preys on ex-cons. He’s wary, then sedated, then trapped, which makes him a human face for the movie’s larger machinery.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the showcase territory of Michael Peña in a tense procedural thriller — a role that lets an actor move from charm to fear to physical helplessness fast. It’s a compact but vivid part for someone who can make a victim feel specific rather than generic.

lead_characters.name: Young Rico
lead_characters.hook: Young Rico is the child version of the protagonist at the exact moment her life fractures. She’s curious, frightened, and emotionally open, which makes the disappearance memory land with real force.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of flashback role that gives a young performer a single, emotionally legible showcase moment, similar to the child-memory material in The Sixth Sense. It’s brief, but it carries the movie’s emotional origin point.

director_appeal.hook: A director who wants to turn surveillance, grief, and cosmic paranoia into one escalating pressure cooker.
director_appeal.fit_profile: First- or second-feature directors with a strong genre short or a festival feature behind them, especially those who like contained suspense, visual rules, and performance-forward horror. This material rewards directors who can make a neighborhood feel like a trap, and who understand how to stage dread through blocking, sound, and reveal rather than scale alone.
director_appeal.detail: The movie gives a director a clean visual grammar — red door, blue door, foil, bell, comet — and then lets that grammar collapse into body horror and institutional conspiracy. It’s especially attractive to filmmakers who can make a contained production feel bigger than its footprint and who know how to keep a thriller legible while it gets stranger.

buyer_appeal.lane: Premium streamer genre lane / elevated horror-thriller
buyer_appeal.detail: The contained neighborhood footprint and small lead ensemble make this playable off a strong script and a credible director, without needing a giant cast or globe-trotting schedule. The comet countdown, conspiracy reveal, and body-horror finale give it a trailer-friendly hook that fits the current streamer appetite for elevated genre with a clear concept.

considerations.area: The middle leans on repeated surveillance beats.
considerations.detail: The stakeout material does a lot of work establishing Rico and Cole, and the red-door/blue-door geography is memorable. A next pass could consider compressing a few of the waiting-and-watching beats so the first discovery inside the house arrives with even more snap.

considerations.area: Watson’s system reveal could arrive a touch earlier.
considerations.detail: The final dungeon explanation lands with force, and the movie already plants enough institutional behavior to support it. One lever would be to seed a slightly clearer hint of Watson’s larger operation before the hospital and support-group material, so the last-act turn feels even more inevitable.

considerations.area: The support-group thread is a strong emotional bridge.
considerations.detail: Rico and James give the movie a human corridor between the case and her mother wound, and that material helps the ending land. The version of the script where that relationship is given one more charged scene earlier could deepen the emotional payoff without changing the plot engine.

considerations.area: The creature finale pushes the effects load upward.
considerations.detail: The foil-lined dungeon, body transformations, and final swarm are all playable, but they do ask for disciplined practical design and a clear effects plan. A production-minded pass could simplify one or two of the creature beats without losing the central reveal or the comet-driven climax.

considerations.area: The brand and institution references are plentiful.
considerations.detail: The script uses a lot of named real-world references in dialogue and scene direction, from FBI and NSA language to consumer brands like Reynolds Wrap, Bud Light, and Minute Maid. A clearance pass would be straightforward, but it’s worth tracking those references early so the production package stays clean.
